title: A regulator has said out loud what the time limit debate keeps missing. It is the feed, not the clock.
finalText:
The European Commission has preliminarily found TikTok in breach of European Union law over the way its For You feed works.

Preliminarily is the Commission's own word, and it has to stay in the sentence. This is a finding published on 6 November 2026 under the Digital Services Act, which TikTok can answer before anything is decided, and it does not prove that the feed has harmed a child or that anything has changed for families in the UK.

I would still read it twice.

The Commission calls it the rabbit hole effect. The more someone engages with a type of content, it says, the more the feed recommends similar material, and that design can be harmful when the content is about sadness, isolation or body image.

That is a regulator describing a design. It is not a study.

But it is about what a child is shown, and my own rules at home were about how long.

A timer can tell me how long a child was on an app. It cannot tell me what kept arriving during that time, what was repeated, or what the feed learned to serve next. Children can spend the same amount of time on the same platform and be shown very different worlds.

So look at the feed.

Sit beside your child for a short scroll and ask what it has been showing them lately, and why they think those things keep coming back. Keep it light. The aim is to make the recommendation system visible enough to talk about.

None of this replaces time limits, platform responsibility or safer design. I build a parent tool, so I am not neutral, and our stage check is three questions about one child and a starting point, with no promise about what happens next.

The source is in the comments.

If more parents and teachers need this distinction, repost it. The conversation should include what fills the time as well as how long the timer ran.

When you last looked at a child's feed, what pattern did you notice?
firstComment:
The European Commission announcement, published 6 November 2026:
https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/commission-preliminarily-finds-tiktoks-you-feed-breach-digital-services-act-harmful-rabbit-holes

The strongest objection is that this is a regulator's preliminary view, not research demonstrating harm. Agreed. TikTok can respond, the decision may change, and the Digital Services Act is European Union law. The useful point is narrower: a personalised feed shapes what fills the time, so a timer alone cannot describe the experience.
